fact_label: Dog breed restriction — dangerous and potentially dangerous dog law
value_raw: Breed-blind at the border — Portugal's entry regime does not reference breed at all, so importing a listed-breed dog is not blocked — but a real, ongoing local ownership regime applies once the dog is kept in the country, for seven named breeds and their crosses: Cão de Fila Brasileiro, Dogue Argentino, Pit Bull Terrier, Rottweiler, American Staffordshire Terrier, Staffordshire Bull Terrier, and Tosa Inu. Requirements: a special license from the local parish civil office (Junta de Freguesia), obtainable when the dog is 3-6 months old and revalidated annually; a completed training course for detention of a dangerous dog; muzzle and a leash no longer than 1 metre in public; mandatory civil liability insurance; sterilization for non-pedigree dogs of these breeds between 4 and 6 months of age (pedigree-registered dogs exempt); reported fines of €500-3,750 for non-compliance. Sources diverge on owner-age specifics: one names 18+ as the license-holder age, a second distinguishes license-holding (18+) from the lower bar to actually walk the dog in public (16+)

Pet import (cat) — species-specific requirement verification
value_raw: Same core EU/DGAV entry framework as dogs (microchip before rabies vaccination, 15-week age floor, titer test waived for listed-country origins including the US, no routine quarantine if compliant, 48-hour PEV advance-notice requirement) — no separate breed-restriction law equivalent to dogs' dangerous-dog statute. fact_label: Pet import cost — entry-point fee and EU health certificate
value_raw: Entry-point veterinary inspection fee (non-EU-origin pets, paid on-site at the airport): €42.25 for one pet, €84.50 for two to five pets. EU health certificate cost: €80-300 if obtained from a Portuguese/EU veterinarian, or roughly $510-560 if obtained from a US veterinarian before departure (covers the exam, certificate preparation, and the US Department of Agriculture's own export-endorsement service, USDA-APHIS)

fact_label: Pet import (dog) — rabies titer / quarantine requirement
value_raw: No rabies antibody titer test required for a dog arriving from a country on the EU's titer-exempt list (the US sits on this tier); a titer test is required only from an unlisted-country origin, drawn 30+ days after first vaccination, and the dog cannot travel until 3 months after the sample-collection date. No routine quarantine for a compliant animal. Portugal's own age floor: entry authorised only for dogs over 15 weeks old (12-week minimum rabies-vaccination age + 21-day validity wait), ISO-compliant microchip implanted before or on the vaccination date, and a 10-day-validity EU health certificate. Mandatory 48-hour advance written notice to the specific Traveller's Point of Entry (Ponto de Entrada de Viajantes, PEV) — Lisbon, Porto, and Faro are the three designated PEV airports. Stated consequence of failed compliance: return to origin or, as a last resort, euthanasia under EU legislation

fact_label: Pet import — governing EU regulatory instrument (2026 update), Portugal-specific confirmation
value_raw: As of 22 April 2026, non-commercial pet movement into/within the EU, including Portugal, runs on Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/131 and Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/705, superseding the 2013-era regulation numbers (576/2013 / 577/2013) most existing pet-relocation literature still cites. Confirmed directly against DGAV's (Direção-Geral de Alimentação e Veterinária, Portugal's competent veterinary authority) own "Na Europa" page, which names both instruments by number. Of Crete's two named 2026 tightenings: (1) the EU pet passport now restricted to owners' EU-member-state habitual residence — CONFIRMED verbatim in DGAV's own text ("emitido no país europeu onde o proprietário do animal reside habitualmente" — issued in the European country where the owner habitually resides); (2) mandatory microchip scan-and-verify at every entry point, replacing spot checks — confirmed as to legal mechanism and Portugal-specific institutional practice (DGAV veterinarians at the Pontos de Entrada de Viajantes, in collaboration with Alfândega/Customs), but DGAV's own text does not use the exact "every entry, replacing spot checks" phrasing found in Crete's source, a narrow residual gap rather than a live doubt about coverage

fact_label: Community & digital nomad network — scale and organization
value_raw: The most organized and largest digital-nomad community of the three researched Portugal locations. Lisbon Digital Nomads, a dedicated volunteer-run community organization, has run continuously since 2017, hosting weekly Thursday drinks meetups plus monthly Lisbon StartUp Drinks and Remote Work Happy Hours — organized, recurring social infrastructure, not just an informal expat chat group. Two large informal networks sit alongside it: the 'Digital Nomads Lisbon' Facebook group (20,000+ members) and the Lisbon Digital Nomads Meetup group (25,000+ members). Coworking spaces with their own resident social scenes (BRIC, Second Home, Selina) function as secondary community hubs beyond the citywide ~16,000-nomad estimate already on file for Lisbon (overview.md)

fact_label: Community & digital nomad network — scale and organization
value_raw: Real but smaller and less internationally hyped than Lisbon's, consistent with Porto's own cost-of-living/gentrification read. The main Facebook group (Digital Nomads Porto) runs at roughly 3,000+ members — deliberately smaller and more actively moderated than Lisbon's much larger groups, per its own stated intent — alongside an 'Expats in Porto' group and a newer, city-hall-backed weekly-events project specifically for digital nomads. At least four dedicated coworking spaces run monthly memberships from ~€110/month; CRU Cowork, in the city's arts quarter, is named specifically for its workshop/exhibition-driven community, distinct from a pure desk-rental space

fact_label: Community — expat demographic composition and Digital Nomad Visa impact
value_raw: Beyond Lagos's own existing seasonal/community-texture narrative (three overlapping populations in one small town): the Algarve region's foreign-resident population is estimated at more than 10% of the total regional population, with British expats forming the largest national group, followed by Germans, Dutch, French, and Scandinavians, and a growing number of Americans/Canadians in recent years. Portugal's own Digital Nomad Visa specifically drove real, measurable Algarve growth: over 9,300 D8 applications nationally between October 2022 and September 2025 helped push the Algarve to 10th place in the Savills Executive Nomad Index 2025 — a real, ranked, comparative data point

fact_label: Income viability — remote work, AI, and the local economy
value_raw: Lisbon is Portugal's strongest hub for outside-income-brought-in via remote work/freelancing (not local-market employment). Freelance/remote day rates run roughly €450-600 nationally, though projects reportedly close faster than before. Portugal's AI job market is growing fast: AI-related roles reported up an estimated 20% year-on-year in 2026, with AI cited as poised to add up to €22 billion to Portugal's GDP nationally, concentrated disproportionately in Lisbon's tech/startup ecosystem — GenAI prompt-engineering and AI-compliance roles named specifically as in-demand. Average pay for a remote AI role in Portugal is cited at roughly €47,802/year (a national, not Lisbon-specific, figure). Distinct from the D8 visa's own €3,680/month income threshold (PT:d8-visa-income-threshold) — this is about earning potential and market depth, not the visa's minimum qualifying bar

fact_label: Income viability — remote work, AI, and the local economy

A comfortable monthly budget for an expat/remote worker in Porto is cited around €1,450-1,950 (rent, groceries, transport, utilities, dining, entertainment) — meaningfully below Lisbon's own equivalent figure in cost-of-living.md, consistent with Porto's own 25-30%-cheaper-housing finding

fact_label: Income viability — a genuinely different, seasonal-tourism-driven shape
value_raw: Named plainly rather than softened: Lagos's own local economy is primarily tourism-driven and seasonal, not a remote-work/tech hub the way Lisbon or (to a lesser extent) Porto are. Tourism directly employs an estimated 70,000 people across the Algarve during peak summer months, and Lagos-specific job postings skew toward hospitality (hotels, tour operators, surf schools), commonly paying €900-1,500/month — low-paying and seasonal by the same sources' own description, not a source of strong local income for a remote worker. The real income opportunity in Lagos, as with Lisbon and Porto, is bringing outside remote/freelance income in rather than earning it locally — the region's 'relaxed lifestyle and reliable internet' is named specifically as the draw for freelancers, not a strong local job market

fact_label: Nature & water adjacency — Tagus estuary and Atlantic beaches
value_raw: Lisbon sits at the mouth of the Tagus river where it meets the Atlantic — the only European capital with genuine Atlantic beaches inside easy reach. More than two dozen Blue Flag beaches lie 15-40 minutes away by public transport (the Cascais/Estoril rail line reaches the first beach towns in under 20 minutes), with the Serra da Arrábida Natural Park across the river mouth adding a second, hillier coastal option to the south. A real surf culture exists along this coast, described by dedicated surf sources as carrying some of Europe's best wave diversity — not just calm swimming beaches

fact_label: Nature & water adjacency — Douro river mouth and Matosinhos beach
value_raw: Porto sits at the mouth of the Douro river (the Foz do Douro district takes its name directly from this — 'foz' means river mouth) where it meets the Atlantic; the riverside/oceanfront district blends walks, gardens, and swimming/watersports directly at the point where river meets ocean. The Atlantic coast continues north to Matosinhos, a distinct beach town about 2km north of Foz and roughly 15 minutes by metro from central Porto — EU-rated water quality, lifeguards June-September, and a genuinely popular summer beach in its own right for residents, not just a Porto day-trip afterthought

fact_label: Nature & water adjacency — Ponta da Piedade and the open-Atlantic Algarve coast
value_raw: Lagos's own coastline is among the most distinctive of any Portugal location researched: the limestone headland of Ponta da Piedade (about 3km from the town center) is widely cited as one of the most photographed stretches of coast in the country — sea caves, arches, and cliff-sheltered coves (Praia Dona Ana, Praia do Camilo). Meia Praia runs nearly 2km of open sand to the east; beyond the headland, the coast opens to the full Atlantic with a genuinely different, wilder character at Porto de Mós, a serious surf beach. A categorically different water-adjacency profile from Lisbon's estuary-plus-nearby-beaches or Porto's river-mouth-plus-Matosinhos shape — direct, dramatic open-ocean coastline within the town itself, not a short trip away

date: 2004-04-29 (Directive 2004/38/EC adopted; transposition deadline 2006-04-30; consolidated text current through amending Directive 2011/24/EU, in force 2011-06-16)
document_conditional_note: Residence beyond three months requires meeting one of several conditions (Directive 2004/38/EC Art. 7): being a worker or self-employed, having sufficient resources plus comprehensive health insurance, being an enrolled student with resources and insurance, or being a qualifying family member of someone who meets one of those. This is an additional, better-secured right some readers can go on to claim -- it is never a condition on the entry/short-stay tier shown above, which is already unconditionally true for up to three months under Art. 6 ("without any conditions or any formalities other than the requirement to hold a valid identity card or passport"). A host state may ask for registration after arrival (Art. 8), but the Directive states plainly that holding a registration certificate "may under no circumstances be made a precondition for the exercise of a right" -- a formality, not a gate.

fact_label: Portugal's passive-income residency visa (D7) documentation shape
value_raw: For Portugal's passive-income residency visa (D7): a savings floor of at least €11,040 (12x the €920/month income threshold), plus 50% for a spouse and 30% per dependent child, mirroring the income threshold's own family add-ons. For pension income specifically (one of D7's three named legal applicant categories, per gov.pt), the documentary standard under Portaria n.º 1563/2007 (as amended by Portaria n.º 760/2009) is a certificate issued by the official entity of the country granting the pension, with an authenticated declaration — a distinct, named standard, cross-corroborated across multiple 2026 practitioner guides, though the Portaria's own full primary text has not been directly verified from source. For ordinary (non-pension) passive income — rental, dividends/investment, IP royalties — no equivalently specific document-format standard (bank-statement look-back period, notarization requirement) was found in available sources beyond the general income-source list itself. Applicants also face Portugal's immigration and asylum agency (AIMA)'s own document-rejection-strict processing environment generally (since April 28, 2025, AIMA rejects any application missing even one required document immediately rather than allowing supplementation) — a process-wide fact, not D7-specific, but directly relevant to how much documentation slack an applicant actually has.

fact_label: D8 Visa documentation shape
value_raw: Savings floor: at least €11,040 (12x D7's own €920/month threshold, since D8's savings requirement is stated as the same figure with the same dependent add-ons), plus the same 50%/30% dependent add-ons. Primary income-proof standard: 'evidence of remote or freelance jobs' (getgoldenvisa.com, re-fetched directly 2026-08-07) — active remote-work invoicing/earnings, not passive-income statements. Process-specific wrinkles worth carrying alongside the document list itself: the visa must be secured through a consulate before arrival (the 'Manifestation of Interest' in-country application loophole is now closed), and D8 processing specifically is taking 6-9 months as of June 2026, driven by backlog at Portugal's immigration and asylum agency (AIMA) — both real, dated, and D8-specific rather than general Portugal-wide facts.

fact_label: Seasonal tourist crowding and accommodation squeeze -- bare claim only, radically simplified after three returns for revision
value_raw: Lagos has a real summer tourist season. Wikipedia (2021 census population 33,494, checked 2026-08-24): 'The influx of visiting tourists and seasonal residents during the summer months increases the population' -- no multiplier, no adverb, no comparison, just 'increases.' nomads.com (checked 2026-08-24): 'summer brings a massive influx of tourists... driving up prices and crowding public areas,' and 'Accommodation becomes hard to find and very expensive during peak season.' Nothing beyond these two plain claims is stated here -- no doubling figure, no named beach, no transit/car-dependency claim.
